That unspaced form is what GPT-2's tokeniser produces when a word is glued to preceding punctuation (an opening parenthesis, quote, em dash, hyphen, slash, underscore or bracket, or a line start) rather than following a space, so its peaks are the first word inside a parenthetical or quotation — 'files (the "Software")', '(with a count)', '(and you)', 'models (which differ)' — and it fires on the token wherever it occurs, including as the first piece of 'theoretical' ('the') or 'however' ('how'). It is inactive on the space-prefixed token of the same word (' the', ' with', ' and' = 0.00) and on the title-case token ('The', 'And', 'With' = 0.00), stays silent on punctuation and digits, and grades with frequency and grammaticality among unspaced words: unspaced function words reach 1.5-3.4 while unspaced content words are weak (water, code, game, table = 0.00; 'people' = 1.26).

At the end of the nineteenth century the harbour town lived almost entirely from fishing. Families whose names still appear on the memorial had worked the same boats for four generations, and the rhythm of the year was set by the tides rather than by any calendar. The school closed during the herring season because every pair of hands was needed on the quay. Visitors who arrived by the new railway expected picturesque cottages and were surprised instead by the smell, the noise and the hard bargaining that went on beside the water.

By the time the council began to discuss a proper road along the shore, the herring had already started to fail. The minutes of those meetings, kept in a careful copperplate hand, record arguments about drainage, lamp posts and the cost of gravel. Nobody in them mentions tourism. What they do mention, again and again, is the difficulty of persuading the railway company to stop more than once a day. Merchants complained that goods arrived late and that visitors who might have stayed for a week came only for an afternoon.

The turning point came quietly. A retired schoolmaster wrote a pamphlet describing the cliffs to the north of the town, and within two summers strangers were walking out to see them with borrowed boots and a printed map. Boarding houses opened in streets that had never housed anyone but fishermen. Old men who had spent their lives at sea ended up explaining knots and weather to people from the city who wrote everything down.

When the war came, the visitors stopped, and the town discovered how much it had come to depend on them. The harbour, the boats and the curing sheds survived, but the trade that had built them did not return. A generation later the council finally voted to restore the quay as a heritage site (the committee finally agreed), and the photographs on the wall still show the same faces that once waited for the fleet.
